lead: A generator's output voltage is not fixed. It rises as the shaft speeds up and falls as the load current rises. The cause is the field: generated emf depends on field flux and speed. A voltage regulator senses the output, compares it with a reference, and adjusts field current to hold voltage steady. Aircraft use three hardware forms: the vibrating-contact regulator, the carbon-pile regulator, and the electronic regulator. The first two are older; the electronic type is standard in generator control units.
prereq: You need: 3.1 for the generator, its field winding and the generator control unit.

sections.h3: The field is the control knob

blocks.text: Generated emf in a DC generator is E = k Φ ω. E is the generated emf in volts, k is a machine constant, Φ is the field flux per pole in webers, and ω is angular speed in radians per second. For a given field current, Φ is roughly constant. Then E rises in direct proportion to speed. At the terminals the voltage is lower than E by the armature resistance drop and by armature reaction. So terminal voltage falls as load current rises.

The regulator cannot change speed. It changes field current I<sub>f</sub>. A small change in I<sub>f</sub> gives a large change in Φ, and so in E. The loop is closed: sense terminal voltage, compare with a reference, drive the field. The quality measure is voltage regulation.

blocks.where: V<sub>no-load</sub> is the terminal voltage at zero load in volts; V<sub>full-load</sub> is the terminal voltage at rated load in volts; the result is a percentage. Smaller is better.

blocks.text: Vibrating-contact regulator. A solenoid coil is connected across the generator output. A spring holds a contact closed. While the contact is closed, full field current flows. When output voltage exceeds the setting, the solenoid pulls the contact open. A series resistance then enters the field circuit, so field current falls and voltage falls. The contact closes again. The cycle repeats many times a second, and the spring tension sets the regulated voltage. The average field current is set by the duty cycle D, the fraction of time the contact is closed. On light-aircraft DC generators it comes as a three-unit regulator: the voltage regulator, a current limiter (a second vibrating contact worked by a series coil, which caps the generator current) and a reverse-current cut-out. Its regulation is coarse, the contact arcs, so it wears and makes radio noise, and it needs periodic cleaning and adjustment.

Carbon-pile regulator. A stack of carbon discs sits between two plates. Its resistance falls as pressure rises. A solenoid works against a spring to vary the pressure, and the pile is in series with the field. Higher voltage pulls the solenoid, reduces pressure, raises pile resistance, and lowers field current. The control is smooth and has no arcing contacts, but the discs still wear slowly, shed carbon dust and drift with age and heat, so it needs periodic adjustment. The pile is also slow to respond. It was used on larger DC generators where smooth control mattered more than speed.

An electronic regulator uses a Zener diode as the reference. A sensing divider scales the output down. An error amplifier compares the scaled output with the Zener voltage. Its output drives a transistor, a thyristor, or a pulse-width modulator that switches the field. Pulse-width control gives a duty cycle D, and the average field current is D × I<sub>field</sub>(max). The loop is fast, has no moving parts and regulates most closely of the three. The same unit adds over-voltage and under-voltage cut-out, over-excitation limiting, and reverse-current protection. Cut-out removes the generator from the bus; it does not regulate voltage.

examples.question: A 28 V DC generator has a field resistance of 10 Ω. The regulator inserts a 20 Ω series resistance when its contact opens. The average field current needed is 1.5 A. (a) Find the duty cycle D, the fraction of time the contact is closed. (b) With no load the output is 28.4 V and at full load 27.6 V; find the voltage regulation.
steps: Contact closed: field current I<sub>closed</sub> = 28 V ÷ 10 Ω = 2.80 A.
Contact open: total field circuit resistance = 10 Ω + 20 Ω = 30 Ω. I<sub>open</sub> = 28 V ÷ 30 Ω = 0.933 A.
Average field current = D I<sub>closed</sub> + (1 − D) I<sub>open</sub>. Put 1.50 A = D(2.80 A) + (1 − D)(0.933 A).

Duty cycle = 0.304 × 100 = 30.4 %. This takes the field current as jumping between 2.80 A and 0.933 A; the field is inductive, so the real current rises and decays along curves and the true duty cycle differs a little, but the average-current method is what the exam expects.
examples.answer: Duty cycle is 30.4 % and voltage regulation is 2.9 %.

traps: Adding the regulator resistance in the load circuit instead of the field circuit.
Treating the vibrating contact as a fixed resistor; it works by duty cycle.
Using no-load voltage in the denominator of regulation; use full-load voltage.
Saying carbon-pile resistance rises with pressure; it falls. And "no contacts" does not mean no wear: the discs wear and drift.
Confusing a cut-out with a regulator; a cut-out removes the generator, a regulator holds voltage.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a voltage regulator?
quiz.a: It holds generator terminal voltage near a set value by adjusting field current as speed and load change.

quiz.q: Why does terminal voltage fall as load current rises?
quiz.a: Armature resistance drop and armature reaction reduce the terminal voltage below the generated emf as load current increases.

quiz.q: A 28 V generator field has R<sub>f</sub> = 12 Ω and the regulator inserts 24 Ω when its contact opens. The average field current needed is 1.2 A. Find the duty cycle.
Why does a vibrating-contact regulator produce radio noise, and what in the regulator causes it?
quiz.a: The contact opens and closes while current flows in the field circuit. Arcing at the contact creates fast voltage and current changes that radiate radio-frequency interference.

quiz.q: Name the three voltage regulator types in this chapter.
Why is a carbon-pile regulator contactless but slow?
quiz.a: It varies resistance by pressure on carbon discs, so there are no switching contacts. The solenoid and the pile have mechanical and thermal lag, so it responds slowly; the discs still wear slowly and need adjustment.

quiz.q: The bus trips on over-voltage although the regulator's adjusting screw has not been touched. Name two faults that could cause it, and say why the over-voltage unit is separate from the regulator.
quiz.a: A lost or open sensing lead (the regulator sees no voltage and drives full field) or a field-drive transistor failed short (full field whatever the error). The over-voltage unit is separate so that one failure in the regulator cannot both cause the over-voltage and stop the protection that clears it.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern generator control units are digital: a microcontroller runs the same sense-compare-drive loop, with PWM field drive and built-in test. Wide-bandgap switches and higher bus voltages such as 270 V DC change the drive stage but not the control principle. Remote sensing at the busbar compensates for cable drop. Search for generator control unit, PWM field regulation, and over-excitation limiter.
